[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing remote teams with 2 vs. 4+ daily synchronous check-ins, measuring team cohesion via validated sociometric surveys and deep work time via digital activity logs — Directly tests the causal claim by manipulating check-in frequency in the specified scope (knowledge-intensive, high interdependence teams) and measuring both mediating mechanisms (meeting fatigue, deep work) and the outcome (cohesion).

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on meeting frequency, meeting fatigue, and team cohesion in distributed work contexts — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple studies to assess the consistency and effect size of the hypothesized relationship, and identifies potential moderators like task interdependence or team size that align with the scope.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling the trade-off between synchronous coordination frequency and deep work time in knowledge-intensive teams — Provides a formal theoretical framework to explore the conditions under which the hypothesized negative effect emerges (e.g., threshold effects, diminishing returns), helping to refine the causal mechanism and scope conditions before costly empirical testing.

scope.domain: teams with high task interdependence and knowledge-intensive work

qualifier.condition: when check-ins exceed four per day

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing team cohesion metrics (e.g., social network density, trust surveys) between remote teams with daily synchronous stand-ups vs. asynchronous check-ins, controlling for task interdependence. — Directly tests whether high-frequency synchronous meetings reduce cohesion via meeting fatigue and lost work time, while isolating the effect from other variables.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote work studies (2020–present) examining the relationship between meeting frequency, perceived meeting fatigue, and team cohesion outcomes, with subgroup analysis for high task interdependence teams. — Aggregates existing evidence across contexts to assess the generalizability and strength of the hypothesized causal chain, and identifies gaps in current research.

[PATH:empirical] Field experiment comparing daily 15-minute stand-up meetings with written agendas vs. no structured check-ins in remote teams with low task interdependence — Directly tests the causal claim that high-frequency structured check-ins strengthen cohesion under the specified scope, while controlling for meeting fatigue and deep work preservation.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote team communication frequency and cohesion, with moderator analysis for agenda structure and time-boxing — Synthesizes existing evidence on the relationship between synchronous check-in frequency and team cohesion, and can reveal whether the predicted effect holds specifically when structural constraints are applied.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of autonomy-threat and coordination rituals in distributed teams (e.g., based on self-determination theory and interaction ritual theory) — Explains the boundary condition: teams with high autonomy needs may perceive frequent check-ins as controlling unless carefully structured, providing a mechanism that could confirm or refute the hypothesis.
